p: The Greek has "mother" where the Hebrew has "his compassion".

readings.w: Masoretic Text; Mur88 (MurXII) shows these words, and 4Q82 (4QXIIg) restores "his compassion"

readings.en: and he ruined a mother on the earth
readings.plain: ruined a mother on the earth

why: The Greek "mother" suggests the translator read the Hebrew rachamav as rechem ("womb"), or took the word loosely; the Hebrew "his compassion" fits the charge of cruelty to a kinsman and agrees with Mur88. The verb shichet means "ruin, destroy, corrupt" (the Greek has elumenato, "ruined"), so the Plain English Translation says "destroyed".
b: The same Greek verse renders le-ad ("forever") as "for a witness" (eis martyrion), and has "he kept his rage for victory". These show a translation with a different sense division, not a different Hebrew text in every case. Modern commentators who prefer to read the next clause as "he kept his anger forever" (a verb for keeping in place of "tore") do so by emendation; the Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic Text.

p: The same consonants can be read "their king" or "Milcom", the god of Ammon.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (pointed malkam); 4Q82 and Mur88 have the same consonants
Reading the same consonants as Milkom (as Jeremiah 49:3 does in the Plain English Translation)
readings.en: Milcom, the god of the Ammonites

readings.orig: οἱ βασιλεῖς αὐτῆς, οἱ ἱερεῖς αὐτῶν

why: The next phrase, "he and his officials together", fits a human king. Jeremiah 49:3 has the god and his priests in a very similar line, and some scholars think Amos meant the god too, but the Masoretic pointing is the oldest evidence.
b: The Plain English Translation's Jeremiah 49:3 reads: "For Milcom will go into exile, / his priests and his officials together." The Greek of Amos has "priests" where the Hebrew has "officials", which looks like influence from the Jeremiah line. The scrolls here only show the consonants, which cannot tell the two readings apart.

t: "My holy name" or "the name of their God"?
p: The Greek changes who owns the name.

readings.plain: profane the name of their God

why: The Hebrew is the oldest witness and is the harder reading, since the LORD speaks of his own name in the first person here.

p: The Greek has Assyria where the Hebrew has Ashdod.
why: The Hebrew is supported by the scroll. Ashdod and Egypt are a natural pair as witnesses from neighbors. Assyria and Egypt are the pair elsewhere in the Twelve, which may have led to the Greek.
b: The herald calls the citadels of Ashdod, a Philistine city, and of Egypt to look at the oppression in Samaria. Assyria and Egypt are the great powers whose conflict decided the age (Hosea 7:11; 12:1), which may explain the Greek.

a: An enemy, all around the land
p: The Hebrew tsar "enemy" and tsor "Tyre" differ by a vowel.

readings.en: An enemy, all around the land
readings.plain: An enemy, all around the land

readings.orig: Τύρος κυκλόθεν ἡ γῆ σου ἐρημωθήσεται
readings.en: Tyre, your land will be laid waste all around
readings.plain: Tyre, your land will be laid waste all around

why: Tyre is not the subject anywhere else in the oracle against Samaria, and the verb "pull down" fits an attacker. The Masoretic Text makes sense as it stands.

a: a scrap of cloth from a couch
t: A corner of a bed, and what?
p: The last words of 3:12 can mean "Damascus", "damask cloth" or something else.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (consonants shared by 4Q78); read as a word for cloth
readings.plain: a scrap of cloth from a couch

readings.w: Masoretic consonants read as the city

why: All the readings are uncertain. The Plain English Translation takes the rare word as a luxury cloth because the furniture list matches 6:4.
b: The Hebrew has bi-fat mittah u-vi-demeshek 'eres. pe'at is "corner" and mittah "bed". demeshek may be the city of Damascus, a word for a rich fabric (the later "damask"), or an Aramaic word for a couch; 'eres is a couch or divan. The Plain English Translation reads "a scrap of cloth from a couch": the luxury furniture of 6:4 is all that will be saved. 4Q78 has the same consonants as the Masoretic Text.

p: The Greek has "the mountain Rimmon" for the unknown word Harmon.
why: No Harmon is known. The Greek suggests a mountain name, but also shows the translator guessing. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew and does not guess the place.

a: lets people know what he is thinking
p: The Greek reads the Hebrew as "announces his anointed to people", a reading some early Christian writers used.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (no scroll preserves the verse)
readings.plain: lets people know what he is thinking

readings.orig: ἀπαγγέλλων εἰς ἀνθρώπους τὸν χριστὸν αὐτοῦ

why: The Hebrew siach means "thought" or "speech" and the Masoretic Text is the only Hebrew witness. The Greek seems to read meshicho "his anointed", or to play on the sound. It is a Christian reading in the fathers; as a Hebrew text it has no support.
b: In the Hebrew it is unclear whether "his" refers to God or to the human being: God tells people what they are thinking, or what he is thinking.

a: The one who made the Pleiades and Orion
t: Two named stars, or no stars?
p: The Hebrew names Kimah and Kesil; the Greek names no stars.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (no scroll preserves the verse)
readings.plain: The one who made the Pleiades and Orion

readings.en: who makes all things and changes them
readings.plain: The one who makes all things and changes them

why: The Hebrew names the two star groups, as Job 9:9 and 38:31 do. The Greek has no star names here; it may be a free rendering of a rare pair of words. Either way the sense changes only in that the Greek loses the sky.
b: The identification of Kimah and Kesil with the Pleiades and Orion is the usual one but is not certain (see the note).

t: Sikkuth or the tent of Moloch?
p: The Hebrew names; the Greek has the tent of Moloch.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (no scroll preserves the verse); read as the name Sikkuth
Masoretic consonants read as common words

why: The Masoretic vowels may be those of "abomination", which marks a god's name. The Greek and Acts read the same consonants as "booth/tent" plus Moloch. The Damascus Document (CD 7) quotes the verse in a different form (a first-person "I will exile" in place of "you will carry") and explains the "booth" as the books of the Law; it is the strongest Hebrew witness to a text other than the Masoretic one.

p: The Greek has a different name for the star god.

readings.w: Greek (Swete); Acts 7:43 has Rhomphan or Rephan in some manuscripts
readings.orig: τὸ ἄστρον τοῦ θεοῦ ὑμῶν Ῥαιφάν
readings.en: the star of your god Rhaiphan
readings.plain: the star of your god Rephan

why: Both names are probably a Hebrew and a Greek spelling of the same Mesopotamian star-god title (Saturn); how the Greek reached "Rephan" is debated.
b: The Hebrew has 'eloheikhem, "your gods", plural in form, and the Plain English Translation follows it: "the star of your gods". The Greek and Acts 7:43 have a singular, "your god".

a: Cross over to Calneh and look
p: The Hebrew names a city, Calneh; the Greek has no city and says "cross over, all of you".

readings.w: Masoretic Text; 4Q82 (4QXIIg) shows the word Calneh
readings.plain: Cross over to Calneh and look

readings.w: The same consonants read as one word (proposed)
readings.plain: Cross over, all of them, and look

readings.en: cross over, all of you, and see
readings.plain: Cross over, all of you, and look

why: The Hebrew place name is visible in 4Q82 and Isaiah 10:9 names Calneh beside Hamath, so the city is a natural reading. The Greek has no place name and may have read the word as "all".
b: The Greek also calls Gath "the strongest of all these kingdoms" where the Hebrew asks whether these kingdoms are better than Israel's. The dating argument that makes 6:2 later than Amos (the fall of Calneh in 738 BC) depends on the place name being right.

a: Does anyone plow there with oxen?
t: Oxen on a cliff, or oxen in the sea?
p: A one-letter change gives "plow the sea with oxen".

readings.w: Masoretic Text; 4Q82 (4QXIIg) shows only "Do they run" (hayeratsun) and "horses if"; the words that decide the question (basela', yacharosh, babbeqarim) are restored
readings.en: or does one plow with oxen
readings.plain: Does anyone plow there with oxen?

readings.w: Proposed reading (dividing the letters as ba-yam baqar)
readings.en: does one plow the sea with oxen
readings.plain: Does anyone plow the sea with oxen?

readings.en: will they be silent among mares
readings.plain: Will they be silent among the mares?

why: No scroll shows the disputed words, so none can be cited for or against the proposed division. The proposed change gives a better parallel to "horses on a cliff", but no manuscript stands behind it, and the Masoretic Text makes sense as it is.

a: the late crop that grows after the king's cutting
t: The king's cutting, or Gog the king?
p: The Greek has "one locust, Gog the king".

readings.w: Masoretic Text; 4Q78 (4QXIIc) shows "the king" (ha-melekh) and the word before it, gizzei, is restored; 4Q82 (4QXIIg) breaks off before the word
readings.plain: the late crop that grows after the king's cutting

readings.orig: καὶ ἰδοὺ βροῦχος εἷς Γὼγ ὁ Βασιλεύς
readings.en: and look, one locust, Gog the king

why: The word that decides between the Hebrew and "Gog" is restored in 4Q78 and missing from 4Q82, so no scroll can be cited for it; the Hebrew rests on the Masoretic Text. The Greek seems to have read the consonants as a name, which ties the locusts to the end-time enemy (Ezekiel 38-39).
b: gizzei ha-melekh is "the king's mowings": the first cutting of grass taken by the king's officers for royal horses (compare 1 Kings 18:5; 1 Samuel 8:14-15). The farmer had only the second growth. The Greek reads the same consonants as a name, "Gog the king", which ties the locusts to Ezekiel 38-39.

p: The rare word anak is read as metal in the Greek.

readings.w: Masoretic Text; 4Q78 (4QXIIc) shows "wall of anak" (anak), and 4Q82 (4QXIIg) shows anak with "wall" restored; Mur88 preserves only the second anak ("in his hand an anak")
readings.en: a wall of anak (plumb line, tin or lead)

why: Wherever the word is visible in the scrolls it is anak; Mur88 does not preserve the first one. The Greek translator took it as a hard metal. A plumb line fits the idea of a test in 7:8.
b: In 7:8 4Q82 has "the LORD" (YHWH) where the Masoretic Text has "the Lord" (Adonay), and 4Q78 has hineh ("look") where the Masoretic Text has hinni ("look, I"); the next word in 4Q78 is restored, so the scroll cannot be cited for "I have set".

a: I am no prophet, and I am no prophet's son
t: "I am no prophet" or "I was no prophet"?
p: The Hebrew has no verb; the Greek chose the past.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, with no verb; 4Q78 and Mur88 show the same words with some letters restored, and none adds a verb
readings.orig: לֹא נָבִיא אָנֹכִי וְלֹא בֶן־נָבִיא אָנֹכִי
readings.en: not a prophet I, and not a prophet's son I
readings.plain: I am no prophet, and I am no prophet's son

readings.orig: Οὐκ ἤμην προφήτης ἐγὼ οὐδὲ υἱὸς προφήτου
readings.en: I was not a prophet, nor a prophet's son
readings.plain: I was no prophet, and I was no prophet's son

why: The Hebrew has no verb, so both are possible, and the grammar does not decide. The Plain English Translation takes the present, as most commentators do today: Amos denies that he is a professional prophet, a member of a prophetic guild, while accepting the LORD's order to speak. The word ki before "a herdsman I" can be "but rather" (which favors the present) or "for" (which favors the past), and the Plain English Translation leaves it unwritten. The past reading makes it a statement about his life before the call.
b: The Greek also has "goatherd" (aipolos) for boqer and "pricking sycamore fruit" for the fig work. Jerome's Latin has the present, non sum propheta.

a: the temple songs will turn to wailing
p: The Greek read one letter differently and got "the ceiling panels of the temple will wail".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (the scrolls are broken here; 4Q82 shows the last letter of the word)
readings.plain: the temple songs will turn to wailing

readings.en: the ceiling panels of the temple
readings.plain: the ceiling panels of the temple will wail

why: Songs turning into wailing is a regular picture in the prophets (8:10). The Greek makes the temple itself cry out.

p: The first word is written "like the light" but the Plain English Translation reads "like the Nile", as the same line does in 9:5.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (no scroll preserves the word)
readings.en: and all of it will rise like the light

readings.w: Read as in 9:5, where Mur88 (MurXII) has the word ka-ye'or
readings.en: and all of it will rise like the Nile
the end will rise like a river

why: The next line says "like the Nile of Egypt" and 9:5 repeats the picture with ka-ye'or, which the Mur88 scroll shows in 9:5; "the earth rises like the light" gives no picture. The Plain English Translation therefore takes the written ka'or as a short spelling of ka-ye'or, as the Greek "like a river" also suggests.
b: The Greek takes kullah ("all of it") as "the end" (synteleia), which differs again from the Hebrew. The Ketiv and Qere on the later verb are in the note.

t: The guilt of Samaria, or its god?
p: A pun or a god's name; the Greek has "propitiation".

readings.w: Masoretic Text; Mur88 (MurXII) agrees, and 4Q82 (4QXIIg) restores the whole phrase

readings.en: by the propitiation (offering for sin) of Samaria
readings.plain: the offering for sin of Samaria

why: The Hebrew is the text of Mur88 and makes sense as an ironic oath. The god Ashimah is a proposal, with no manuscript behind it.

t: "The way to Beersheba" or "your god, Beersheba"?
p: The Greek has a god Beersheba.

readings.w: Masoretic Text; 4Q82 and Mur88 have the word "way" (derekh)

why: Two scrolls have derekh. A pilgrimage road to Beersheba fits 5:5. Some scholars read derekh as dodekha ("your beloved", a god) after the Greek and a parallel at Ugarit; this is a proposal.

a: they may take possession of the remnant of Edom
t: Possess Edom, or seek the LORD?
p: The Hebrew has the people possess what is left of Edom; the Greek, which Acts 15 follows, has "the rest of humankind may seek".

readings.w: Masoretic Text; Mur88 (MurXII) has "the remnant of Edom" with the word "Edom" intact, the verb "possess" is restored
readings.en: that they may possess the remnant of Edom
readings.plain: they may take possession of the remnant of Edom

readings.en: that the rest of humankind may seek
readings.plain: the rest of humankind may seek

why: The Hebrew is the only text in Hebrew and Mur88 has it. The Greek differs by two small things, one letter in the verb (yidreshu "seek" for yirshu "possess") and the vowel letter in Edom/adam "human"; it may rest on a different Hebrew text or a free reading. Acts 15 follows the Greek of this verse (with changes elsewhere, see the note) and its argument does not need the Hebrew wording.
b: The Hebrew verb yirshu has the letters y-r-sh-w; the Greek verb "seek" matches yidreshu, y-d-r-sh-w, with an added d. The Hebrew edom (aleph-dalet-vav-mem) and adam (aleph-dalet-mem) differ by the vowel letter vav, which was often not written in early texts. Views: (1) the Greek translator had a different Hebrew text (so a reading as old as the Hebrew one); (2) the Greek translator interpreted a text like the Masoretic one, ending the national hope for Edom and widening it to all people; (3) James in Acts 15 used the Greek because it was the text in his hearers' hands. All three are held by serious scholars. See the card on this passage. Acts 15 follows the Greek of Amos in the 9:12 verb and subject, but not everywhere: Acts 15:16 opens "After these things I will come back" where the Greek Amos has "On that day", uses "come back, build again, set upright" where the Greek has "raise up, build again", adds "the Lord" after "seek" and "all" after "these things", and closes with "known from ages past" (15:18), which has no counterpart in Amos 9:12.
